title: My daily routine
goal: Build sentences that have a verb, describe your daily activities, and see how one Arabic verb changes according to who does the action.
bekal: form present-tense verbs for every person
describe the sequence of a whole day's activities

dialogs.title: حِوَار — كَيْفَ تَقْضِي يَوْمَكَ؟
dialogs.intro: In the campus canteen. Laila asks Budi about his daily habits.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: What time do you usually get up?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: أَسْتَيْقِظُ فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ، ثُمَّ أُصَلِّي.
lines.id: I get up at five, then I pray.
lines.literal: I-wake-up at the-hour the-fifth, then I-pray.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: And what do you do after that?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: I have breakfast and drink tea.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Do you go to campus by bus?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لَا، أَمْشِي. اَلْجَامِعَةُ قَرِيبَةٌ مِنْ بَيْتِي.
lines.baca: laa, amshii. al-jaami'atu qariibatun min baitii.
lines.id: No, I walk. The campus is close to my house.
lines.literal: no, I-walk. the-campus near from house-my.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: What are you studying this semester?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: I'm studying grammar and literature. And you?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: أَنَا أَدْرُسُ التَّرْجَمَةَ، وَأَعْمَلُ فِي الْمَسَاءِ.
lines.id: I study translation, and I work in the evenings.
lines.literal: I I-study the-translation, and I-work in the-evening.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Sometimes. But I love my job.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: هٰذَا هُوَ الْمُهِمُّ. أَنَا أَيْضًا أُحِبُّ الدِّرَاسَةَ هُنَا.
lines.baca: haadhaa huwal-muhimm. anaa aiḍan uhibbud-diraasata hunaa.
lines.id: That's what matters. I love studying here too.
lines.literal: this it the-important. I also I-love the-study here.

notes: **An Arabic verb already contains its subject.** أَدْرُسُ on its own already means "I study" — you don't have to say أَنَا. If أَنَا is added anyway (as in أَنَا أَدْرُسُ), it adds emphasis: "*I'm* the one studying". English always needs the pronoun; Arabic only uses it for stress.
**The prefix tells you who, not the ending.** أَ- for I, تَـ for you and she, يَـ for he, نَـ for we. These four letters cover almost all of everyday conversation.

**تَدْرُسُ has two meanings.** "You (m) study" and "she studies" — the form is exactly the same. Context separates them, and misunderstandings do sometimes happen even between native speakers. To make it clear, the pronoun is added: هِيَ تَدْرُسُ.

**Speaking to a woman, the verb ends in ـِينَ.** أَلَا تَتْعَبِينَ؟ — "don't you (f) get tired?". This follows directly from the اِسْمُكِ and حَالُكِ you've used since unit 1: Arabic distinguishes a male and a female "you" wherever it can.

**The object takes a fatha.** أَدْرُسُ النَّحْوَ, أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ, أُحِبُّ عَمَلِي. The fatha at the end marks the word as the **object** of the verb. At A1 you aren't expected to add it yourself in every sentence, but learn to recognize it — it's clearly audible.
**بِالْحَافِلَةِ — بِ marks the means.** "By bus". Same pattern: بِالسَّيَّارَةِ (by car), بِالْقِطَارِ (by train), بِالْقَلَمِ (with a pen), بِيَدِي (with my hand).

**Verbs are negated with لَا, not لَيْسَ.** لَا أَفْهَمُ (I don't understand), لَا أَعْرِفُ (I don't know), لَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ (I don't drink coffee). Remember the split: لَيْسَ for sentences without a verb, لَا for sentences with a present-tense verb.

**ثُمَّ and وَ are not the same.** وَ simply joins ("and"), ثُمَّ shows sequence in time ("then, afterwards"). There's one more, even tighter: فَ ("and then, right away") — دَخَلَ فَجَلَسَ ("he came in and sat down", with no pause).
**لٰكِنِّي = لٰكِنَّ + ي.** "But I". لٰكِنَّ is always followed by a noun or an attached pronoun, never directly by a verb — just like إِنَّ in unit 5.

grammars.title: The present tense (al-fi'l al-muḍaari')
body: One verb, eight forms. What changes is the **prefix**; some forms also add an ending. The example below uses دَرَسَ (study), whose middle letter takes a damma: يَدْرُسُ.
after: If you can only manage four, learn these: **أَ- (I), تَـ (you), يَـ (he), نَـ (we)**. Those four prefixes cover most conversation.
One form covers two tenses at once: أَدْرُسُ means "I study" (habit) **and** "I am studying". Arabic doesn't separate the two the way English does.

grammars.title: The shifting middle vowel
body: The unpredictable part of an Arabic verb isn't the prefix but **the vowel on the middle letter** in the present tense. It can be damma, fatha or kasra, and it can only be learned along with the word.
after: So **always learn verbs in pairs**: كَتَبَ — يَكْتُبُ, not just كَتَبَ. From those two forms every other form can be derived without guesswork.
The good news: this only applies to basic three-letter verbs. Derived verbs (أَرَادَ — يُرِيدُ, تَكَلَّمَ — يَتَكَلَّمُ) follow fixed patterns that don't need to be learned one by one.

blocks.text: Notice that some of these are already full sentences, not just words. That's the best way to learn them: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ also teaches you that ذَهَبَ takes إِلَى, not some other preposition.

blocks.title: The first verbs you must know fluently
items: These ten cover most everyday sentences, and all of them have already appeared in this book: ذَهَبَ (go), جَاءَ (come), أَكَلَ (eat), شَرِبَ (drink), دَرَسَ (study), عَمِلَ (work), سَكَنَ (live), فَهِمَ (understand), عَرَفَ (know), أَرَادَ (want).
The drill that pays off fastest: take one verb a day and build eight sentences with eight different subjects. Ten days, ten verbs, and conjugation stops feeling like a table.

head: Question
Pronunciation
Meaning
rows: What are you doing? / What do you do?
What time do you get up?
How do you get to the office?

blocks.text: Notice the difference between مَا and مَاذَا: مَا is used before a noun (مَا اسْمُكَ؟), مَاذَا before a verb (مَاذَا تَفْعَلُ؟). Using مَا in front of a verb is one of the most typical beginner mistakes, because English uses the one word "what" for both.

blocks.title: Questions that make people enjoy talking to you
items: Open questions keep a conversation alive much longer than yes/no questions. Compare هَلْ تُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ؟ ("do you like coffee?") with مَاذَا تَشْرَبُ عَادَةً؟ ("what do you usually drink?").

Three questions that always get a conversation going in the Arab world: مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ بِالضَّبْطِ؟ ("where exactly are you from?"), مَاذَا تُحِبُّ فِي مَدِينَتِكَ؟ ("what do you like about your city?"), and كَيْفَ حَالُ الْعَائِلَةِ؟ ("how's the family?").

exercises.prompt: Change the verb to match the subject given.

items: We go to campus by bus.
Where do you work? (to a woman)
They read books in the library.

exercises.prompt: Negate these sentences. Watch out: لَا or لَيْسَ?
Describe your day from waking up to going to bed, in at least eight sentences. Link them with ثُمَّ and بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ.
items: What time do you get up, and what do you do next?
What do you have for breakfast?
How do you get to work or class?
What do you do during the day?
What time do you get home?
What do you do in the evening?

answers: أَدْرُسُ — نَشْرَبُ — تَذْهَبِينَ — تَكْتُبُ — يَعْمَلُونَ — تَقْرَأُونَ

أَسْتَيْقِظُ فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ. — هِيَ تَدْرُسُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ. — نَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْجَامِعَةِ بِالْحَافِلَةِ. — أَيْنَ تَعْمَلِينَ؟ — لَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ. — هُمْ يَقْرَأُونَ كِتَابًا فِي الْمَكْتَبَةِ.
لَا أَفْهَمُ الدَّرْسَ. — لَيْسَ هُوَ طَالِبًا. — لَا نَذْهَبُ إِلَى السُّوقِ. — لَيْسَ عِنْدِي وَقْتٌ. — هِيَ لَا تَعْمَلُ فِي الْمَسَاءِ.

Example: أَسْتَيْقِظُ فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ ثُمَّ أُصَلِّي — أَتَنَاوَلُ الْفُطُورَ وَأَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ — أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ بِالسَّيَّارَةِ — أَعْمَلُ فِي الْمَكْتَبِ مِنَ الثَّامِنَةِ إِلَى الرَّابِعَةِ — أَرْجِعُ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ فِي الْخَامِسَةِ — أَتَعَشَّى مَعَ عَائِلَتِي ثُمَّ أَقْرَأُ كِتَابًا
wave: Reread the unit 7 dialogue. Now you can recognize يَبْدَأُ and تَشْرَبُ as verbs with a subject, not just sounds.
